content.theory:
Everything in a running program lives at a **memory address**. Every variable occupies bytes in RAM, and `&variable` gives you the *address* of that variable. A **pointer** is a variable whose value is an address:

```cpp
int x = 42;
int* p = &x;   // p stores the address of x
std::cout << *p << std::endl;   // 42 — dereference p
```

`int* p` reads as "p is a pointer to int". The `*` in front of the pointer *dereferences* it: it follows the stored address and gives you the value living there. So `*p` and `x` are the same variable — write `*p = 7` and `x` becomes 7.

### Why pointers matter

Raw arrays are why pointers exist in C. An array variable **decays** to a pointer to its first element when you pass it to a function, so `void sum(int* arr, int n)` silently accepts arrays. Pointers are also how you do **dynamic memory**: `new` returns a pointer to memory requested at runtime, which is the foundation of linked lists, trees, and hash tables. Modern C++ wraps this with smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`) that free the memory automatically.

### nullptr and safety

A pointer can be *null* — it points to nothing. Initialize pointers (or set them to `nullptr`) and always check before dereferencing:

```cpp
int* p = nullptr;
if (p) {              // false — safe check
    std::cout << *p;
}
```

Dereferencing a null pointer is a crash, so the check matters.

### Pointer vs reference

| Feature | Pointer `int* p` | Reference `int& r` |
|---|---|---|
| Can be reassigned | Yes | No |
| Can be null | Yes | No |
| Explicit dereference | `*p` | None — implicit |

A pointer is a separate variable holding an address; a reference is an alias that always refers to the same object. Use references by default in modern C++, and pointers when you need to express "no object" with `nullptr`.

exercise.instruction: Write the program: declare `int x = 42`, create a pointer `int* p = &x`, then print the value the pointer points to using `*p`.
hints: Hint 1: Declare the variable first: int x = 42;
Hint 2: Create the pointer: int* p = &x; — the & takes the address of x
Hint 3: Print the pointed-to value: std::cout << *p << std::endl;

quiz.question: What does *p do?
options: Dereferences p to give the value at that address

quiz.question: Why check a pointer against nullptr before dereferencing?
options: Dereferencing a null pointer crashes the program
